posts.title: Why we still steam the towels
posts.excerpt: A microwave is faster. A steamer is kinder to the skin, and to the morning.
posts.content:
Every morning at half past nine the towels go into the old copper steamer behind the counter. By ten they are hot all the way through, evenly, with no dry corners that sting.

A steamed towel stays warm for the two minutes it takes to soften a beard. That is the whole secret of a close shave without a red neck afterwards.

posts.title: Forty strokes on the strop
posts.excerpt: The razor from 1962 is still sharp because someone strops it every single morning.
posts.content:
Genji hangs the leather strop from the hook by the mirror and draws the razor along it forty times, spine first, twenty on each side. It takes three minutes and nobody talks to him while he does it.

For the shaves we use a fresh blade in a holder; the old razor is kept for the neck line of a cut, where its weight helps the hand stay steady.

posts.title: A first haircut on a Saturday morning
posts.excerpt: The baker’s son was four, and he wanted to sit in the purple chair, not on a booster.
posts.content:
He arrived with his father at ten, the first customer of the day, holding a small paper bag of bread for us. Mio let him spin the chair once before she began.

It took twenty minutes, a lot of talking about trains and one lollipop. We kept a small lock of hair in an envelope for his mother, as Genzo used to do.
